## Covariates

The six buoy-measured water/air conditions used by the forecast
models, all sourced from A01's sensors:

::: {.covariates-table}
| Covariate  | Description         | Sensor | Depth        | Units |
|------------|----------------------|--------|--------------|-------|
| temp_1m    | Water temperature    | sbe37  | 1m           | °C    |
| temp_20m   | Water temperature    | sbe37  | 20m          | °C    |
| cond_1m    | Conductivity         | sbe37  | 1m           | mS/cm |
| cond_20m   | Conductivity         | sbe37  | 20m          | mS/cm |
| sal_20m    | Salinity             | sbe37  | 20m          | psu   |
| air_temp   | Air temperature      | met    | -3m (above surface) | °C |
:::

## Trajectory features

Beyond the six sensor readings above, the bloom-day models use a
few extra features to help describe where a bloom is in its life
cycle:

::: {style="max-width: 900px; margin: 0 auto; font-size: 19px;"}
- **Days since bloom started**: how many days it's been since
  chlorophyll first crossed the bloom threshold. Lets the model
  treat day 3 of a bloom differently from day 10 of the same one.
- **Rise rate so far**: the average daily increase in chlorophyll
  since the bloom began. A rate that's flattening out or turning
  negative is a strong signal the bloom is already near or past its
  peak.
- **Day of year**: captures seasonality, so a spring bloom is
  treated differently from a summer or fall one.
- **Recent forecast error**: how far off today's observed
  chlorophyll is from a simple "yesterday's trend continues" guess,
  as a measure of current volatility.
- **Each covariate's 7-day trend**: today's water/air condition
  minus its value a week ago, so the model knows whether conditions
  are warming, cooling, etc., not just their current level.
- **Hourly chlorophyll volatility**: how much chlorophyll swung
  up and down within a single day's hourly sensor readings (its
  standard deviation, high-low range, and trend), capturing
  short-term noise that a single daily average would miss.
:::

## Forecast pipeline

::: {style="max-width: 800px; margin: 0 auto 3rem auto; overflow: hidden;"}
```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'flowchart': {'wrappingWidth': 400}}}%%
flowchart TD
    A["Today's chl-a observation + 6 covariates:<br/>&bull; Water temp (1m, 20m)<br/>&bull; Conductivity (1m, 20m)<br/>&bull; Salinity (20m)<br/>&bull; Air temperature"]
    A --> Q(("Is today's chlorophyll above 5 ug/L?"))

    Q -->|"Yes, bloom in progress"| BM["4 Random Forests trained on past blooms:<br/>&bull; Days since bloom started<br/>&bull; Rise rate so far<br/>&bull; Day of year<br/>&bull; Recent forecast error<br/>&bull; Each covariate's own 7-day trend<br/>&bull; Hourly chl-a volatility"]
    BM --> BM1["Draw 100 values for remaining peak magnitude"]
    BM --> BM2["Draw 100 values for remaining duration"]
    BM --> BM4["Draw 100 values for rise fraction"]
    BM --> BM3["Draw 100 values for decline rate"]
    BM1 --> TRAJ["Build 100 trajectories: rise to each predicted peak<br/>at its predicted rise rate, then decline at its predicted fall rate,<br/>plus daily noise"]
    BM2 --> TRAJ
    BM4 --> TRAJ
    BM3 --> TRAJ
    TRAJ --> OUT["100-member, 7-day chlorophyll forecast"]

    Q -->|"No, calm"| CFC["6 Random Forests predict each covariate daily up to 7 days ahead, 100 members each"]
    CFC --> CM["Random Forest draws tomorrow's chl-a change for each member<br/>from its own value + its 6 forecasted covariates"]
    CM -->|"Repeat for each lead time (t) using each<br/>member's chl-a from the previous day (t-1)"| CM
    CM --> OUT
```
:::

::: {style="max-width: 900px; margin: 0 auto; font-size: 19px;"}
The forecast is an ensemble of 100 members instead of a single line.
Each Random Forest is a quantile regression forest, so for a given set
of inputs it estimates the full distribution of the value it is
predicting, not just the average. It does this by collecting the past
observations that landed in the same leaves as the current inputs across
all of the forest's trees, weighting each by how often it shares a leaf.
To draw one member's value, a random quantile level between 0 and 1 is
picked and the value at that quantile of the weighted distribution is
used (inverse transform sampling). What gets sampled depends on the
model:

- **Bloom day**: each member draws its own peak, duration, rise
  fraction, and decline rate, then builds its own bloom trajectory
  from those four numbers. The draws are centered on the 0.7 quantile
  instead of the median, because the median underestimates large
  blooms. Each trajectory also gets random day-to-day noise (about 20%
  on day 1, growing to about 40% on day 7), since real bloom days swing
  more than a smooth rise and decline.
  
- **Calm day**: the draws happen at every step. Each member gets its
  own randomly drawn covariate forecasts and its own randomly drawn
  daily change in chlorophyll, building on that member's own previous
  day.

The spread between members is the forecast's uncertainty, and the
average across members is the forecast. On the Today page, the shaded
bands and bars show the average plus or minus one standard deviation
across the 100 members. All 100 members are
saved for every forecast date in the Ecological Forecasting Initiative
(EFI) standard format, one row per member per day.
:::

## Water column stratification

::: {style="max-width: 900px; margin: 0 auto; font-size: 19px;"}
The stratification figures on the Today page use the CTD sensors on the A01
mooring at 1m, 20m, and 50m, as daily means from the NERACOOS ERDDAP server.

- **Density difference**: density (sigma-t, in kg/m3) at 20m minus density at
  1m, shown year-to-date against the typical range for that time of year.
  Values near zero mean the water column is well mixed, and higher values mean
  lighter surface water is sitting on denser deep water.
- **Water column outlook**: density by depth for the latest observed day and
  the 7-day forecast. Each sensor's density is forecast the same way as the
  covariates (a Random Forest uses today's value and day of year to predict
  tomorrow's, run as a 100-member ensemble, and the ensemble mean is shown).
  Between sensors, density is drawn as a straight line by depth, and it is
  held constant above 1m and below 50m, so the colors between the white dots
  are interpolated, not measured.
- **Mixed layer depth**: the orange line on each column. It is the depth where
  density first exceeds the density at 1m by a threshold, found by linear
  interpolation between sensors. If no sensor exceeds the threshold, the water
  is reported as mixed down to the deepest sensor (>50m).

**Choice of threshold.** For profile data, the standard criterion is a density
increase of 0.03 kg/m3 from a near-surface value (de Boyer Montégut et al.
2004). A larger criterion of 0.125 kg/m3 (Levitus 1982)
is also widely used. A01 has only three sensors and daily means, and on
well-mixed winter days the density difference between 1m and 20m is already
about 0.04 kg/m3 (the January median since 2008), so 0.03 kg/m3 would label
most winter days as stratified. This page uses 0.125 kg/m3.

Because the sensors are 19m apart, depths between 1m and 20m are
interpolated, and the estimate is best read as an index of how thick the
surface layer is rather than a measured depth. In summer it comes out around
2m, shallower than the 6.5m July climatology for the western Gulf of Maine
from profile data (Cai et al. 2021). In winter it can only say the layer is
deeper than 50m, where profile data give about 78m for January (Cai et al.
2021).

**References**

- Cai, C., Kwon, Y.-O., Chen, Z., and Fratantoni, P. (2021). Mixed layer depth
  climatology over the northeast U.S. continental shelf (1993-2018).
  *Continental Shelf Research*, 231, 104611. (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.csr.2021.104611)
- de Boyer Montégut, C., Madec, G., Fischer, A. S., Lazar, A., and Iudicone, D.
  (2004). Mixed layer depth over the global ocean: An examination of profile
  data and a profile-based climatology. *Journal of Geophysical Research*, 109,
  C12003. (https://doi.org/10.1029/2004JC002378)
- Levitus, S. (1982). *Climatological Atlas of the World Ocean*. NOAA
  Professional Paper 13, U.S. Government Printing Office.
:::

## Bloom thresholds

::: {style="max-width: 900px; margin: 0 auto; font-size: 19px;"}
A day counts as a bloom when the daily mean chlorophyll at 3m is above 5
ug/L. Blooms are labeled mild (5 to 10 ug/L), moderate (10 to 20 ug/L), or
severe (above 20 ug/L). The 5 and 20 ug/L cut-offs come from two US
assessments of coastal chlorophyll-a. EPA's National Coastal Condition Report
II rated surface chlorophyll-a at individual sites as good below 5 ug/L, fair
from 5 to 20 ug/L, and poor above 20 ug/L (US EPA 2004, Table 1-4, p. 10), and
NOAA's National Estuarine Eutrophication Assessment classified the maximum
surface concentration over a typical annual cycle as low (up to 5 ug/L),
medium (above 5 to 20), high (above 20 to 60), or hypereutrophic (above 60)
(Bricker et al. 1999, Appendix A). The 5 ug/L value is also within the range
of strong spring bloom averages in Massachusetts Bay, up to about 6 ug/L in
northwest Massachusetts Bay in 2000 (Jiang et al. 2007). At A01, daily means
exceed 5 ug/L on about 18% of days and 20 ug/L on about 0.1% of days
(2005-2025), and chlorophyll fluorescence at the buoy peaked above 20 ug/L in
late April and early May 2023, during the exceptional *Tripos muelleri* bloom
(MWRA 2024). The 10 ug/L boundary between mild and moderate is not a
published threshold. It is a local split, roughly the 96th percentile of
daily values at A01. These benchmarks were developed for site samples or
annual maxima rather than daily buoy fluorescence, and high chlorophyll does
not mean a bloom is harmful, which MWRA tracks separately through species
counts (MWRA 2024).

**References**

- Bricker, S. B., Clement, C. G., Pirhalla, D. E., Orlando, S. P., and Farrow,
  D. R. G. (1999). National Estuarine Eutrophication Assessment: Effects of
  nutrient enrichment in the nation's estuaries. NOAA, National Ocean Service,
  Special Projects Office and National Centers for Coastal Ocean Science,
  Silver Spring, MD. (https://library.oarcloud.noaa.gov/noaa_documents.lib/NOS/NCCOS/eutrophication_report_1999.pdf)
- Jiang, M., Zhou, M., Libby, S., and Hunt, C. D. (2007). Influences of the
  Gulf of Maine intrusion on the Massachusetts Bay spring bloom: A comparison
  between 1998 and 2000. *Continental Shelf Research*, 27(19), 2465-2485.
  (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.csr.2007.06.009)
- Massachusetts Water Resources Authority (2024). *2023 Water Column
  Monitoring Results*. Environmental Quality Department.
  (https://www.mwra.com/media/file/2023-water-column-monitoring-results-2024-11)
- US Environmental Protection Agency (2004). *National Coastal Condition
  Report II*. EPA-620/R-03/002. Office of Research and Development and Office
  of Water, Washington, DC.
  (https://19january2021snapshot.epa.gov/sites/static/files/2014-10/documents/nccriicomplete.pdf)
:::

## Development

::: {style="max-width: 900px; margin: 0 auto; font-size: 19px;"}
Random Forest wasn't the only model type tried. Earlier development
screened four model types against each other:

- **ARIMA**: a classic time-series model using only chlorophyll's own
  past values, with no water/air covariates. A simple, useful
  benchmark, but it can't take advantage of any buoy observations
- **XGBoost**: a gradient-boosted tree ensemble, conceptually similar
  to Random Forest but builds trees sequentially, each correcting the
  last one's errors.
- **Dynamic GAM (dGAM)**: a generalized additive model that captures
  smooth, nonlinear relationships between covariates and chlorophyll.
- **Random Forest**: an ensemble of many independent decision trees,
  each trained on a random subset of the data and covariates, then
  averaged together.

Rather than guessing which covariates mattered, every combination of
model type and covariate subset (drawing from the full pool of buoy
and weather-forecast covariates) was cross-validated
against each other (about 237,000 model/covariate combinations in
total). Random Forest came out with the lowest cross-validated error: 
RMSE of about 0.27, compared to roughly 0.30 for
XGBoost, 0.38 for dGAM, and 0.77 for the plain ARIMA baseline.

The same search is also how the covariates were chosen: water
temperature, conductivity, salinity, and air temperature consistently
ranked among the best-performing combinations, while other candidates
that were tried, like mixed-layer depth and current speed, didn't make
the cut. This was validated by a few full test runs with these covariates
to confirm that there was no missing signal from other unincluded covariates.

Early versions of the forecast produced a single line per day.
The current version produces a 100-member ensemble, so the
uncertainty comes directly from the forecast itself.

For more details, see full Documentation in the BloomBoard GitHub (https://github.com/cami-webb/BloomBoard)
:::
